interest:
I am interested in AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs), large
multimodal models (LMMs), foundation models, retrieval-augmented generation,
research agents, and automated scientific discovery methods that can be
useful for astronomy and astrophysics.

Prioritize papers that could help with:
1. JWST imaging/spectroscopy analysis, especially high-redshift galaxies,
   AGN, and little red dots
2. astronomical source classification, anomaly detection, morphology,
   deblending, photometric redshifts, SED fitting, spectral fitting, or
   uncertainty estimation
3. multimodal models that combine images, spectra, catalogs, tables, text, or
   literature
4. LLM agents for literature review, data analysis, coding, scientific
   workflows, or reproducible research
5. methods that could transfer to large survey data from JWST, Roman, Euclid,
   Rubin/LSST, HST, ALMA, or multi-wavelength catalogs

Deprioritize generic NLP, chatbots, robotics, games, social media, medicine,
finance, or benchmark-only papers unless the method clearly transfers to
astronomical research workflows.

papers.title: Rethinking Image Processing for the Age of AI: A Problem-First Framework for Scientific Progress
papers.abstract: Modern AI has greatly expanded the capabilities of image processing. However, the ready availability of powerful models, public datasets, and benchmark leaderboards has also en- couraged a model-first research pattern: researchers increasingly begin with an available architecture and optimize it on a public benchmark, rather than beginning with the underlying real-world imaging problem. This can produce impressive benchmark results without necessarily improving our understanding or solution of the real problem. This paper argues for a problem-first approach that distinguishes the physical imaging problem, solution principle, statistical estimator, and computational implementation, while clarifying what modern AI can achieve and which fundamental problems remain unsolved. Through case studies of super- resolution and low-light enhancement, we show how benchmark datasets may define tasks that differ substantially from the real-world problems they are intended to represent, and why performance improvements must be interpreted within the conditions under which they are obtained. We propose a six-stage workflow that places problem formulation, image acquisition, information-loss analysis, assumptions, ambiguity, and evaluation before model and dataset selection. The paper also proposes clearer standards for evidence, reproducibility, uncertainty, and claims of state-of-the-art performance. More fundamentally, it calls for a change in research culture and education so that future researchers learn to understand imaging problems deeply and use modern AI to achieve genuine scientific and technical advancement.
papers.Reasons for match: Advocates for problem-first research in image processing, directly relevant to developing AI methods for astronomical imaging with clear scientific goals.
papers.Short digest: This paper critiques model-first research in image processing and proposes a problem-first framework that distinguishes physical imaging problems, solution principles, estimators, and implementations. The main idea is to prioritize problem formulation and information-loss analysis before model selection, with case studies in super-resolution and low-light enhancement. For astronomy, this is highly relevant because JWST imaging and spectroscopy often require careful problem definition (e.g., deblending, SED fitting) before applying AI models. A workflow could involve using this framework to design AI-based source classification or morphology analysis with explicit assumptions and uncertainty quantification. The caveat is that the paper is conceptual, not providing new algorithms, so it serves as a methodological guide rather than a ready-to-use tool.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check for concrete examples of how to apply the six-stage workflow to an imaging problem, which could be adapted to JWST data.
Look for discussion of uncertainty estimation and reproducibility standards that could inform astronomical AI pipelines.
Verify if the paper addresses multi-band or spectral data, which is common in astronomy.

papers.title: Hyperspectral Diffusion Equivariant Imaging (HyDiff-EI): A Self-supervised Framework for Hyperspectral Image Inpainting
papers.authors: Shuo Li , Mike Davies , Mehrdad Yaghoobi
papers.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Machine Learning (cs.LG)
papers.abstract: A novel Hyperspectral diffusion Equivariant Imaging (HyDiff-EI) framework for solving the hyperspectral image (HSI) inpainting problem has been presented here. Unlike conventional diffusion-based methods that rely on large-scale pretraining, HyDiff-EI is a test-time optimization framework that learns directly from a single corrupted HSI acquisition. This makes it flexible for different sensor configurations and particularly well-suited for practical remote sensing scenarios where large annotated hyperspectral datasets are limited. To address the ill-posed nature of unsupervised inpainting, we embed equivariant consistency constraints within the diffusion process. By leveraging the inherent geometric symmetries and intrinsic characteristics of HSIs, HyDiff-EI bridges the gap between generative diffusion modeling and self-consistent physical priors. We empirically show that coupling diffusion modeling with equivariant priors substantially enhances noise robustness and generalizability. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets including Chikusei, Botswana, and EMIT demonstrate that HyDiff-EI offers remarkable inpainting quality over existing self-supervised and diffusion-based algorithms in both noiseless and noisy cases.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly addresses hyperspectral image inpainting with self-supervised diffusion, relevant to JWST spectral data and missing data imputation.
papers.Short digest: This paper proposes a test-time optimization framework for hyperspectral image inpainting, learning from a single corrupted acquisition without large pretraining. It embeds equivariant consistency constraints into a diffusion process to leverage geometric symmetries, improving noise robustness and generalization. For astronomy, this could help fill missing or corrupted spectral channels in JWST or ALMA data, especially when labeled datasets are scarce. A concrete workflow would be applying HyDiff-EI to a single JWST hyperspectral cube to inpaint bad pixels or gaps. The main caveat is that the method is designed for remote sensing images, so adaptation to astronomical data may require careful handling of different noise models and spatial scales.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the equivariant constraints are applicable to astronomical symmetries (e.g., rotational or translational invariance in galaxy images).
Look for quantitative comparisons on noisy data to assess robustness for faint astronomical sources.
Verify whether the method scales to large 3D cubes typical of JWST MIRI or NIRSpec IFU observations.

papers.title: Syntax vs. Semantics: How Transformers Learn Deep Dependencies
papers.abstract: Large Language Models demonstrate remarkable syntactic fluency, yet the optimization dynamics governing their acquisition of deep semantic dependencies remain poorly understood. We propose a mechanistic framework that models this learning process as a competition between Surface Statistics and Deep Semantics. Our theoretical analysis identifies a ``Gradient Starvation" phenomenon where the error signals for sparse semantic dependencies are actively suppressed during early optimization. This suppression impedes the learning of structural reasoning and causes its emergence to manifest as a sudden phase transition. Furthermore, this framework offers a mechanistic basis for the effectiveness of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) strategies. By externalizing intermediate reasoning steps into concrete tokens, CoT effectively bypasses the suppression regime inherent to implicit reasoning. We validate these findings across scales ranging from toy transformers to production models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B). Finally, guided by this theory, we propose a topology-aligned contrastive objective that explicitly rectifies the gradient geometry. Experiments on variable binding tasks demonstrate that our method achieves an improvement that is over 2x larger than that obtained via standard cross-entropy fine-tuning.
papers.Reasons for match: Mechanistic understanding of transformer learning and CoT effectiveness could inform LLM-based scientific reasoning, but the paper is theoretical.
papers.Short digest: This paper proposes a framework where transformers learn deep dependencies through competition between surface statistics and deep semantics, explaining gradient starvation and CoT benefits. The main idea is that CoT bypasses suppression of sparse semantic signals. For astronomy, this could help design better prompts or training for scientific reasoning tasks that require deep understanding. It might be useful for improving LLM agents on complex astrophysical reasoning. Check if the proposed contrastive objective can be applied to astronomy-specific tasks.
Full-text inspection checklist: Look for experiments on variable binding tasks that might resemble scientific reasoning.
Check if the gradient starvation phenomenon is relevant to training on sparse astronomical features.

papers.title: SAGE: Variate-Wise Semantic Augmentation for Vision-Language Time Series Forecasting
papers.subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
papers.abstract: Time series forecasting models operate on raw numerical sequences, lacking the semantic knowledge that domain experts implicitly leverage, such as the physical meaning of each variable, its statistical behavior, and its temporal dynamics. Recent efforts to bridge this gap fall into two camps. Some rely on large language models at inference time, which is computationally expensive. Others apply uniform textual prompts at the dataset level, ignoring the heterogeneous semantics across individual variates. We propose SAGE (Seeing and Augmenting with Grounded Encoding), an end-to-end CLIP-based framework that jointly models temporal, cross-variable, textual, and visual information. The CLIP text encoder processes frequency-enhanced patches and variable tokens, while gated residual paths inject variable-specific descriptions and statistical descriptors. In parallel, the frozen CLIP vision encoder aligns rendered series with temporal representations through a training-only contrastive objective. This dual use of CLIP adds complementary semantic and visual supervision without placing an LLM in the forecasting loop. Across eight long-term benchmarks and M4, SAGE achieves state-of-the-art accuracy. Ablations confirm complementary gains from multimodal alignment and variable-level knowledge.
papers.Reasons for match: Combines vision-language models with time series forecasting, relevant to multimodal analysis of astronomical time series (e.g., light curves) with textual metadata.
papers.Short digest: This paper proposes a CLIP-based framework for time series forecasting that integrates temporal, cross-variable, textual, and visual information without using an LLM in the loop. The main idea is to use a frozen CLIP vision encoder to align rendered series with temporal representations and a text encoder to process variable descriptions, adding semantic supervision. For astronomy, this could help forecast light curves of variable sources using auxiliary text (e.g., object descriptions) and images (e.g., cutouts). A workflow might involve predicting future photometric observations of AGN or transients using multi-wavelength light curves and catalog metadata. The caveat is that the method is benchmarked on generic time series, so adaptation to astronomical data with irregular sampling and noise is needed.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the method handles irregularly sampled time series, common in astronomy.
Look for details on how textual descriptions are generated for variables, which may need domain-specific adaptation.
Verify the computational cost of the CLIP-based alignment for large survey datasets.

papers.title: Retrieval Heads Meet Vision: Uncovering How VLMs Locate and Extract Visual Information
papers.authors: Chanho Park , Daehyeon Choi , Jihyun Lee , Minhyuk Sung
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can locate an image region referred to by a text prompt and route the corresponding visual evidence to the output, yet the internal mechanism behind this behavior is not understood. Inspired by retrieval heads in large language models, we ask whether VLMs contain an analogous mechanism for visual retrieval. We answer affirmatively by introducing Visual Retrieval Heads (VRHs), a small subset of attention heads (about 1.7-2.6%) that are causally responsible for grounding text descriptions to image regions. To find them, we recast existing head-scoring methods under a unified design space over query tokens, key aggregation, and cross-sample aggregation. We then show that scoring attention from output prediction tokens with a sum over the ground-truth referent region most reliably identifies causal heads. Across eleven VLMs and five referring-expression benchmarks, masking only the top 20 VRHs reduces grounding accuracy by up to 80 percentage points, while masking the same number of random heads has little effect. Beyond replicating the causal-sparse-universal triad established for text retrieval heads, VRHs exhibit several properties not previously reported: they generalize across visual reference tasks, remaining causal on attribute, spatial, counting, and visual-math benchmarks despite being discovered through bounding-box prediction; they are functionally specific, preserving output format while corrupting localization; and they are architecturally shared, transferring causally across VLMs that share an LLM backbone but differ in vision encoder, projector, and instruction tuning.
papers.Reasons for match: The paper investigates how VLMs retrieve visual information, which is directly relevant to multimodal models for astronomy, especially for grounding text to image regions in astronomical images.
papers.Short digest: This paper introduces Visual Retrieval Heads (VRHs), a small subset of attention heads in vision-language models that are causally responsible for grounding text descriptions to image regions. The main idea is to identify these heads using a unified scoring method and show that masking them degrades grounding accuracy. For astronomy, this is relevant because VLMs are used for tasks like describing astronomical images or locating objects based on text queries. A concrete workflow could involve using VRHs to improve interpretability and reliability of VLMs for astronomical image analysis. The paper provides insights into how VLMs work, which could help in developing more robust multimodal models for JWST data.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the VRH discovery method is applicable to VLMs fine-tuned on astronomical data.
Look for any discussion on the transferability of VRHs across different vision encoders, which is relevant for adapting to JWST images.
Assess whether the findings can inform the design of better grounding models for astronomical source identification.
